translationRepairs: His father, Liu Gu, served as an aide to the Chancellor.

父喈 names the father 喈; Liu Gu is not in the Chinese and contradicts the given name Jie.
A cockfight raised disaster in the state of Lu.
難興魯邦 says disaster arose in Lu; nearly ruined invents averted ruin the source does not state.
He beat wife or children on the spot for fault—such was his severity.
He beat wife or children on the spot for fault—such was his fairness.
其公正如此 names fairness or impartiality; severity inverts the historian’s stated quality.
Eventually permitted, he retired as supernumerary minister with carriage rails before his gate and another million in silver.
Eventually permitted, he retired as supernumerary minister with carriage rails before his gate and another million in cash.
復賜錢百萬 is a further grant of cash, not silver.
So Ji An died in provincial exile and Dong Zhongshu sank to tutoring a prince.
So Ji An died in Huaiyang and Dong Zhongshu was reduced to chancellor of a feudal lord.
汲黯死于淮陽 is death at Huaiyang, not exile; 諸侯之相 is chancellor to a feudal lord, not tutoring a prince.
He soon impeached Wang Yun—Wang Cui—Dong Ai and a dozen more.
He soon concurrently served as palace assistant and memorialized the removal of the vice director, the Prince of Dong'an You, along with Wang Cui, Dong Ai, and more than ten others.
The source names 御史中丞, 尚書僕射, and 東安公繇; Wang Yun is invented and the offices were dropped.
When Liu Yao struck Luoyang Tun commanded defense as Pacifying Army general.
When Liu Yao struck Luoyang, Tun was made General Who Pacifies the Army, granted a staff of authority, and put in command of the city’s defenses.
The original omits 假節 and 都督城守諸軍事; the proposal still omits both appointments and only retitles the generalship.
=Tun courtesy name Changsheng—upright with his father's manner.
Tun, courtesy name Changsheng, was upright with his father's manner.
The leading “=” is a lemma marker on 暾字長升, not part of the sentence.
After Wu fell he shared credit with his brother Yu, who gained a pavilion marquisate.
After Wu was pacified, for He Jiao’s merit in planning counsel his younger brother Yu was granted the rank of Marquis of Runan Pavilion.
以參謀議功 credits He Jiao’s planning; 賜弟郁爵汝南亭侯 grants the pavilion marquisate to the younger brother, not shared credit.
The younger Xun Kai snubbed Wu Mao’s refusal of his patronizing friendship.
Xun Kai of Yingchuan, younger than Mao and a son of Emperor Wu’s paternal aunt, prided himself on noble kinship, wished to befriend Mao, was refused, and therefore resented him.
荀愷欲與茂交，距而不答，由是致怨: Kai sought the tie, Mao refused, and Kai resented him; the original reverses who snubbed whom.
Loyal and blunt, he advised Emperor Wu on everything.
Loyal and upright, he took the altars of the state as his own charge; the emperor prized and favored him and consulted him on most government affairs.
忠正 is loyal and upright, not blunt; the sentence also has 以社稷為己任, 器而昵之, and 政事多諮焉.
The emperor made Ren Kai heir tutor—blocking Jia’s scheme to exile rivals.
The emperor followed and made him junior tutor to the heir, remaining palace attendant as before; Chong’s plan did not succeed.
The source records 太子少傅, 侍中如故, and 充計畫不行; it does not mention exiling rivals.
Favored at court, Jia Chong craved control while Ren Kai moved with He Jiao and Zhang Hua—rival patrons split the faction map.

Favored by the emperor, Jia Chong wished to monopolize fame and power, while Yu Chun, Zhang Hua, Wen Yong, Xiang Xiu, He Jiao and their like all befriended Kai, and Yang Yao, Wang Xun, and Hua Yi were those Chong held dear, so factional cliques flared.
The Chinese names 庾純、張華、溫顒、向秀、和嶠 on Kai’s side and 楊珧、王恂、華廙 on Chong’s; the original drops most of them.
The heir feigned muteness in a grass hut so his brother stole the title.
When Hui’s father died and mourning was completed, Hui returned to his village, built a grass hut, and feigned muteness so that Shu obtained the inherited noble rank.
恢父終，服闋 is the father’s death and the end of mourning; 淑得襲爵 is inheritance, not theft, and the original omits the return home.
Late Wei he served Prince Zhao’s chief clerk.
Late in Xianxi he served as chief clerk to Emperor Wen, the minister of state.
咸熙末 and 文帝 are right against Late Wei and Prince Zhao, but 文帝相國主簿 makes Emperor Wen himself the 相國; “to Emperor Wen’s minister of state” invents a separate chancellor.
Late Xiandi—became Prince Wen’s minister-of-state chief clerk.
Late Xianxi—became Emperor Wen’s minister-of-state chief clerk.
咸熙 is the era Xianxi, not Xiandi; 文帝 is Emperor Wen, not Prince Wen.
He urged removing Xun Xu—Zhong Hui’s kinsman—from Prince Zhao’s staff during Shu revolt.
When Zhong Hui rebelled in Shu, Guo Yi urged removing Xun Xu—Hui’s nephew, raised in Hui’s house and then an aide of Emperor Wen—from that staff.
從甥、少長會家, and 文帝掾 must replace kinsman and Prince Zhao, but leaving the characters 從甥 in the idiomatic English is unnatural.
Touring the provinces with Huangfu Tao he earned promotion to colonel of the gates—Marquis of Linhai.

With Huangfu Tao and Xun Gao he held credentials, toured inspecting customs, and on return, his report meeting with approval, was transferred to colonel of the city gates and advanced to Marquis of Linhai.
The proposal rightly restores 荀暠 and 持節循省風俗, but still omits 奏事稱旨 and 進爵, which explain the promotion and the advance in rank.
He urged retiring Wang Xiang—the emperor honored Wang Xiang and ignored the memo.
He memorialized to dismiss Grand Guardian Wang Xiang for long illness; an edict favored Xiang and shelved Guang’s memorial.
太保 is Grand Guardian; 奏請免之 after 久疾廢朝 is a request to dismiss, not a generic retirement, and 寢光奏 is shelving the memorial.
For helping purge Yang Jun he gained a ten-thousand-household marquisate—rich bounty—and titles for kin.

For merit in executing Yang Jun he was enfeoffed Marquis of Xicheng with ten thousand households and ten thousand bolts of silk; his younger brother Feng became Marquis of Pingqing and his elder brother’s son Kui Marquis Within the Pass.
The source names 西城侯, 弟逢平卿侯, and 兄子逵關中侯 with 邑萬戶 and 絹萬匹; the original erases those persons and titles.
Court pressure failed—He Pan pleaded sickness.
Minister of Ceremonies Cheng Can and General of the Left Bian Cui urged him to take the post; an inner edict grew stern, but Pan claimed illness and would not rise.
太常成粲 and 左將軍卞粹 urged him, then 中詔又加切厲; the original omits both named officials.
First magistrate of Yewang—Yang Hu often visited—Yi sighed: "Uncle Yangzi why must diminish Guo Daye!"
First he was magistrate of Yewang; Yang Hu often visited; Yi sighed: "Why should Uncle Shuzi rank below Guo Daye!"
何必減郭大業 means why must Shuzi rank below Daye; diminish as a transitive verb misreads 減, and 叔子 is Shuzi.
petty rulers like Gong Huan exhaust even sages;
Gong and Huan in power were more than even a great sage could endure;
共驩在位 names two figures Gong and Huan occupying power, not one petty ruler Gong Huan.
Wu Gai kept Wei loyalty; Cui Hong praised Xi Shen; Liu Tun courted Wang Mi; He Pan answered Prince Lun—character shows in crisis.
Wu Gai kept Wei-minister resolve; Cui Hong loved Xi Shen's way; Changsheng urged honor for Wang Mi; He Pan obeyed Zhao Lun's order—a gentleman is seen in the crisis.
愛郤詵之道 is loving Xi Shen’s way; 長升勸王彌之尊 urges honor, not courting; 何攀從趙倫之命 is obedience to Zhao Lun’s order.
Great enterprise not Yang—Yuanbao mocked Jia.
大業 is Guo Yi’s courtesy name, in parallel with 元褒; it is not the noun great enterprise.

unresolvedReferences.description: The Metropolitan Governor who vetoed the Henan impeachment is an unnamed office-holder, not individuated.
The Governor of Henan targeted for impeachment is unnamed.
The six-year metropolitan-governor tenure lacks an explicit Western end date.
Zheng Mao's own calendar year for becoming Minister of Works is not given.
Duke Wu of Zheng is dated only by age over eighty, with no calendar year.
Ji An's death at Huaiyang and Dong Zhongshu's reduction lack source calendar years.
Xingfu cited as a Zhou precedent is not further identified or dated.
三王 (the Three Princes) are a collective of allied princes, not individuated in this chunk.
The sitting 太子 who attended the western palace under Hui is not named; recorded as an unnamed heir distinct from Hui.
永平初 posthumous canonization of He Jiao cannot be mapped because Hui’s Yongping (AD 291) precedes the stated death in 元康二年 (AD 292).
帝不納 after 楊駿執政 is the sitting emperor (historically Hui) but is unnamed; not emitted as a separate person.
Houshi Guang’s death year is not stated beyond dying in office after promotion to Shaofu.
Houshi Xuan’s succession and Xuantu prefecture have no reign year after Guang’s undated death.
Houshi Shi’s succession and Dongguan prefecture have no reign year after Xuan’s undated death.
Chen Shou, Yan Yi, and Fei Li’s decade-plus boycott and clearing have no reign year.
Changsheng is identified in the idiomatic English as Liu Tun; the owned Chinese gives only the courtesy name.
Daye is a courtesy name parallel to Yuanbao; the owned units do not give the corresponding personal name.
